# Module 14: Multidimensional Arrays And Stencil Computation

::: notes
This module uses a tested numerical refactoring to introduce ndarray. Keep the
mathematics simple and make the ownership of each view explicit.
:::

## Module Arc

- Establish a tested loop-based baseline
- Represent a field with `Array2`
- Select array regions with borrowed views
- Express a stencil with `Zip`
- Reuse storage with double buffering
- Broadcast coordinates into a Gaussian field
- Move scientific parameters into TOML
- Reconstruct a matrix from an OpenBLAS-backed SVD
- Verify that the refactoring preserves behavior

::: notes
The example belongs near the end of the course because it combines ownership,
methods, errors, testing, and numerical constraints.
:::

## Three Stages, One Numerical Core

```text
source-code/heat-diffusion/
|-- naive/
|-- ndarray-features/
|-- configurable/
`-- test_consistency.sh
```

- Explicit indices
- Array views and `Zip`

The naive implementation already stores its data in Array2. "Naive" refers to

## The Five-Point Stencil

```text
                 up
                  |
left ---- center ---- right
                  |
                down
```

```text
new = center + alpha * dt
      * (up + down + left + right - 4 * center)
```

::: notes
The outer grid points are fixed boundary conditions, so only the interior is
updated.
:::

## Stability Is An Application Constraint

```text
alpha * dt <= 0.25
```

- Unit grid spacing
- Explicit two-dimensional scheme
- Checked before the simulation starts

::: notes
Rust prevents invalid memory access here, but it cannot infer numerical
stability. This distinction matters in scientific software.
:::

## Owned 2D Storage

```rust
let grid = Array2::<f64>::zeros((grid_size, grid_size));
let (rows, cols) = grid.dim();

let center = grid[[rows / 2, cols / 2]];
```

- Shape belongs to the array
- Storage is rectangular
- Default layout is row-major

::: notes
Contrast this briefly with `Vec<Vec<f64>>`, where rows are separate allocations
and can have different lengths.
:::

## Baseline: Explicit Indices

```rust
for row in 1..rows - 1 {
    for col in 1..cols - 1 {
        new_grid[[row, col]] = self.grid[[row, col]]
            + self.alpha * dt
                * (self.grid[[row + 1, col]]
                    + self.grid[[row - 1, col]]
                    + self.grid[[row, col + 1]]
                    + self.grid[[row, col - 1]]
                    - 4.0 * self.grid[[row, col]]);
    }
}
```

`source-code/heat-diffusion/naive/src/heat_diffusion.rs`

::: notes
Open the real implementation in the editor. The loop is direct and
beginner-readable, which makes it a good reference implementation.
:::

## `s!` Describes A Region

```rust
let interior =
    grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 1..cols - 1]);
```

```text
all rows:       ..
one row:        0
interior rows:  1..rows - 1
```

::: notes
The macro builds slice information; slice then creates a view that borrows the
array. No element data is copied.
:::

## Mutable Boundary Views

```rust
self.grid
    .slice_mut(s![0, ..])
    .fill(boundary_temperature);

self.grid
    .slice_mut(s![.., 0])
    .fill(boundary_temperature);
```

- Select one boundary
- Borrow it mutably
- Apply one operation to the region

::: notes
Show the corresponding loops in the naive version. The slice formulation
states which region may be mutated.
:::

## Circular Hot Spot

```rust
for ((row, col), temperature) in spot.indexed_iter_mut() {
    let dr = row.abs_diff(spot_radius);
    let dc = col.abs_diff(spot_radius);

    if dr.pow(2) + dc.pow(2) <= spot_radius.pow(2) {
        *temperature = spot_temperature;
    }
}
```

::: notes
The mutable view covers the smallest square containing the circle. Its indices
are local to that view, so the radius is also the local center coordinate.
:::

## Five Aligned Views

```rust
let center = grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 1..cols - 1]);
let up     = grid.slice(s![0..rows - 2, 1..cols - 1]);
let down   = grid.slice(s![2..rows,     1..cols - 1]);
let left   = grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 0..cols - 2]);
let right  = grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 2..cols]);
```

::: notes
All five views have shape (rows - 2, cols - 2). At any shared view index, they
refer to one point and its four neighbors.
:::

## `Zip` Walks Them Together

```rust
Zip::from(self.next_grid.slice_mut(
        s![1..rows - 1, 1..cols - 1],
    ))
    .and(center)
    .and(up)
    .and(down)
    .and(left)
    .and(right)
    .for_each(|new, &c, &u, &d, &l, &r| {
        *new = c + factor * (u + d + l + r - 4.0 * c);
    });
```

::: notes
Use the real source for the complete closure. Zip handles aligned traversal;
the code still states the numerical formula explicitly.
:::

## Borrowing Shapes The Design

- Input views borrow `grid` immutably
- The output view borrows `next_grid` mutably
- Distinct fields can be borrowed at the same time
- An in-place stencil would change later inputs

::: notes
This is the ownership lesson. The algorithm naturally needs an old state and a
new state, and Rust makes those roles visible.
:::

## Double Buffering

```rust
pub struct System {
    grid: Array2<f64>,
    next_grid: Array2<f64>,
    alpha: f64,
}
```

```rust
std::mem::swap(&mut self.grid, &mut self.next_grid);
```

- Two allocations, reused for every step
- Current state and next state stay separate

::: notes
The fixed boundaries are initialized in both arrays. Only the interior is
overwritten during each step.
:::

## Fuse The Convergence Reduction

```rust
let new_value = c + factor * (u + d + l + r - 4.0 * c);
max_change = max_change.max((new_value - c).abs());
*new = new_value;
```

- Compute the update
- Measure its change
- Store it in one traversal

::: notes
This removes the extra pass that compared old and new grids. It is still
straightforward because max_change is a scalar local to the sequential Zip.
:::

## Return A Borrowed Array View

```rust
pub fn get_grid(&self) -> ArrayView2<'_, f64> {
    self.grid.view()
}
```

- Read-only access
- Shape and stride metadata
- Cannot outlive `self`
- No element copy

::: notes
Callers that only index or iterate barely change. The return type makes the
borrowed array interface explicit and does not transfer ownership.
:::

## Third Stage: Structured Runs

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Parser)]
struct Args {
    #[arg(short, long, value_name = "FILE")]
    config: PathBuf,

    #[arg(long)]
    show: bool,
}
```

- Scientific parameters move to TOML
- `--show` remains an operational choice
- A file gives the run a reviewable identity

::: notes
The motivation is not only argument count. Nested parameter groups,
alternative model choices, and reproducibility make a configuration file more
appropriate.
:::

## Configuration Mirrors The Domain

```toml
[grid]
size = 21
background_temperature = 0.0
boundary_temperature = 20.0

[material]
thermal_diffusivity = 0.1

[solver]
time_step = 0.01
max_steps = 25
tolerance = 1.0e-12
```

::: notes
Open one of the real files under configurable/configs. Contrast the grouped
tables with the flat command line from the first two implementations.
:::

## One Table, Two Variants

```rust
#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "kebab-case")]
enum InitialCondition {
    UniformDisk {
        temperature: f64,
        radius: usize,
    },
    Gaussian {
        peak_temperature: f64,
        sigma: f64,
    },
}
```

- The `type` field selects a variant
- Each variant requires only its own parameters

::: notes
This is a concrete tagged-enum use. Serde rejects fields that do not belong to
the selected variant because the source also uses deny_unknown_fields.
:::

## Gaussian Coordinates

```text
row squared: (rows, 1)
col squared: (1, cols)
sum:         (rows, cols)
```

```rust
let radius_squared = &row_squared + &col_squared;
```

- Singleton axes are broadcast
- The result covers the complete grid
- No nested coordinate loop

::: notes
Draw the shapes before showing the addition. This is a small example where
broadcasting is clearer than manually repeating row and column coordinates.
:::

## Map Radius To Temperature

```rust
let amplitude = peak_temperature - background_temperature;
let denominator = 2.0 * sigma.powi(2);

self.grid.assign(
    &radius_squared.mapv(|r2| {
        background_temperature
            + amplitude * (-r2 / denominator).exp()
    }),
);
```

- Peak at the center
- Symmetric radial decay
- Fixed boundaries applied afterward

::: notes
The Gaussian is evaluated over the complete field. The domain still enforces
its configured outer boundary temperature.
:::

## Parse, Then Validate

- `Deserialize` checks TOML structure and types
- `deny_unknown_fields` catches misspellings
- Validation checks finite values and ranges
- Stability remains an application constraint

```text
TOML text -> Config -> validated Config -> System
```

::: notes
Separate structural parsing from scientific validation. A syntactically valid
floating-point value can still be an invalid time step or Gaussian width.
:::

## Layout And Performance

- Row-major is the default for owned `Array2`
- Views may be strided and non-contiguous
- Syntax alone does not establish performance
- Benchmark representative release builds

::: notes
Do not claim that Zip is automatically faster. The refactor first improves the
array-level expression and removes repeated allocation; measurement remains
necessary.
:::

## Which Crate?

| Need | Starting point |
|---|---|
| NumPy-like arrays, slices, views | `ndarray` |
| Vectors, matrices, transformations | `nalgebra` |
| Dense linear algebra performance | `faer` |
| Existing native linear algebra stack | `ndarray-linalg` |

::: notes
This is orientation, not an exhaustive ecosystem comparison. Dependency and
deployment constraints may decide the practical choice.
:::

## Compact SVD Shapes

```text
A = U Sigma V^T

A:       (m, n)
U:       (m, k)
Sigma:   (k, k)
V^T:     (k, n)

k = min(m, n)
```

::: notes
Use the 4-by-3 matrix in source-code/svd. Ask participants to predict all four
shapes before opening the implementation. The example selects the OpenBLAS
backend explicitly.
:::

## Reconstruct With `dot`

```rust
let (u, singular_values, vt) = matrix.svd(true, true)?;
let u = u.expect("U was requested");
let vt = vt.expect("Vt was requested");

let k = singular_values.len();
let sigma = Array2::from_diag(&singular_values);
let reconstructed = u
    .slice(s![.., ..k])
    .dot(&sigma)
    .dot(&vt.slice(s![..k, ..]));
```

- `from_diag`: vector to diagonal matrix
- `dot`: matrix multiplication

::: notes
The named U and Vt bindings keep the borrowed views alive through both matrix
multiplications. Connect the dimensions on the previous slide to each dot
product.
:::

## Measure Reconstruction Error

```rust
let difference = &reconstructed - &original;

let max_error = difference
    .iter()
    .fold(0.0_f64, |max, &x| max.max(x.abs()));

let frobenius_error =
    difference.mapv(|x| x * x).sum().sqrt();
```

```{.bash}
cd source-code/svd
cargo run
cargo test
```

::: notes
Do not promise identical final digits across BLAS implementations. The unit
test checks both errors against a tolerance of 1e-12.
:::

## Module Takeaways

- Arrays own data; views borrow regions
- Mutable views make write regions explicit
- `Zip` aligns several same-shaped views
- Broadcasting builds the Gaussian coordinate field
- Double buffering fits stencil semantics
- Tagged enums model alternative configurations
- TOML files make scientific runs reproducible
- A compact SVD combines a factorization with matrix multiplication
- Numerical comparisons need a stated tolerance
- Tests protect both scientific properties and CLI behavior

::: notes
Close by connecting this example back to ownership: the borrowing rules are
not incidental here; they express the lifetime and mutation constraints of the
numerical algorithm.
:::
